lead: TypeScript is JavaScript plus type annotations. A compiler reads the annotations before the code runs, reports mismatches, then removes type annotations. Interfaces and type aliases leave no run-time trace; a non-const enum does become a JavaScript object. The browser receives plain JavaScript. It exists because JavaScript waits until run time to show a wrong argument or a misspelled property; TypeScript moves those mistakes to the editor and the build. Angular projects use it by default, and React projects often add it. You write .ts files, run tsc, and get .js files. Types help autocomplete and refactoring, but they leave no trace at run time.
prereq: You need Unit 3 for variables, functions, ES6 classes and modules.

blocks.text: JavaScript checks types when a line runs. A wrong argument can sit in a rarely used branch until a user reaches it. TypeScript adds annotations and a compiler, tsc, that reads the whole file first. A mismatch is reported before you run. tsc exits with a non-zero status; with noEmitOnError in tsconfig.json it also skips writing app.js. For an exam answer, the call fails to compile — it is a type error.

You write app.ts and run npx tsc. The compiler reads tsconfig.json. Two settings matter. target says which JavaScript version to emit, for example ES2017. strict turns on a group of checks, including strictNullChecks, which keeps null and undefined out of types unless you allow them. The output is app.js. Interfaces, type aliases and annotations leave no run-time trace, but a non-const enum does: it becomes an ordinary JavaScript object, so Size.Small exists at run time. A const enum is inlined and leaves nothing. That is why most types cannot be tested at run time.

The editor uses the same information. After you type user., it offers id, name and email. A misspelled user.nmae is marked before you save. Plain JavaScript would run add('2', 3) and return '23'; TypeScript rejects the call because a string is not assignable to a number. The check is static: it happens before execution.

An annotation follows a name with a colon: let n: number = 7. Common types are number, string, boolean, number[] or Array<number> for an array of numbers, and [string, number] for a tuple whose first item is a string and second is a number. The angle-bracket form is the generic form; both array forms are equivalent. A tuple fixes order and length.

any turns checking off for that value. Avoid it: it spreads, because every property access on an any is allowed. unknown is the safe version. You may store any value in an unknown, but you must narrow it with typeof or a check before use. never is the type of a function that cannot return, such as one that always throws. void is the return type of a function that returns nothing.

A union lists allowed types: 'small' | 'large' accepts only those two strings. A literal type is a single value used as a type. An optional property carries ?: email?: string means the property may be missing or undefined. readonly stops assignment after creation: readonly id: number. Under strictNullChecks, null and undefined are not members of every type. string does not include null. You add | null when null is legal and check for it before use.

A function annotation gives parameter types and a return type: function add(a: number, b: number): number { return a + b; }. a and b are numbers; the value after the colon is the return type. Optional parameters use ? and must come after required ones: greet(name: string, title?: string). Default parameters use =: greet(name: string, title = 'Mr'). A function type is written (a: number, b: number) => number. It describes a value that is a function.

An interface names the shape of an object: interface User { id: number; name: string; email?: string }. A value satisfies it by having the required properties with the right types. TypeScript is structural: the name User does not matter, the shape does. A class or object literal with id: number and name: string is accepted wherever User is expected. This differs from Java, where a class must declare implements.

A type alias gives a name to any type: type Id = number | string. Interfaces can extend: interface Admin extends User { role: string }. An index signature allows extra keys of one type: interface Scores { [name: string]: number }. An enum names a set of constants. enum Size { Small, Large } gives Small = 0 and Large = 1. A string enum writes the values: enum Size { Small = 'small', Large = 'large' }.

A class can mark members public, private, protected and readonly. public is the default. private is visible only inside the class. protected is visible in subclasses too. readonly is set once. A class implements an interface and must provide its members: class Person implements User { constructor(public id: number, public name: string) {} }. The public in the constructor creates and assigns a property.

Generics let one function or class work with many types while keeping the link: function identity<T>(x: T): T { return x; }. The angle brackets declare T as a type parameter. identity<number>(5) returns 5 as a number; TypeScript can infer it from identity(5). A simple Box<T> stores one value: class Box<T> { constructor(public value: T) {} }. TypeScript infers types from values: let n = 7 infers number. Annotate at boundaries, such as exported functions, parameters and shared object shapes. Do not annotate what is already clear; do annotate an empty array, const names: string[] = [], because [] alone infers never[] under strict settings.

figure.caption: tsc reads the annotations first: add('2', 3) is stopped with error TS2345, while add(2, 3) passes, is emitted to app.js with every type erased, and returns 5 in the browser.

spec.aria: Flowchart: app.ts goes into tsc, which sends add('2', 3) down to error TS2345 and sends add(2, 3) down to app.js with types erased, then to the browser where it returns 5.

examples.question: Consider this TypeScript: function add(a: number, b: number): number { return a + b; } and interface User { id: number; name: string; email?: string }. (a) Does add(2, 3) compile, and what does it return? (b) Does add('2', 3) compile? What would plain JavaScript return for '2' + 3? (c) Does { id: 7, name: 'Ravi' } satisfy User? Does { id: '7', name: 'Ravi' } satisfy User?
steps: add(2, 3): both arguments are number. The call compiles and returns 2 + 3 = 5.
add('2', 3): the first argument is string '2'. A string is not assignable to number, so tsc reports error TS2345. There is no output because the call does not compile.
Plain JavaScript skips types. '2' + 3 joins to '23'.
For User, { id: 7, name: 'Ravi' }: id is number, name is string, email is optional. The shape matches User, so it is accepted.
For User, { id: '7', name: 'Ravi' }: id is string. User requires number, so tsc reports error TS2322 on id.
examples.answer: add(2, 3) returns 5; add('2', 3) is a type error (TS2345); plain JavaScript gives '23'; the first User object is accepted and the second is rejected (TS2322).
examples.output:
add(2, 3) → 5
add('2', 3) → error TS2345: Argument of type 'string' is not assignable to parameter of type 'number'.
{ id: '7', name: 'Ravi' } → error TS2322: Type 'string' is not assignable to type 'number' (on id).

traps: An interface or type alias is not a value, so it cannot appear on the right of instanceof, and you cannot write typeof SomeInterface. typeof works only on a real variable, e.g. typeof x === 'string', which is exactly how you narrow an unknown.
any switches checking off for everything it touches. A single any can hide the bug exactly where you stopped typing, so prefer unknown and narrow it.
readonly is a compile-time rule only. It does not freeze the object at run time; JavaScript can still change the property.
A numeric enum uses numbers by default: Size.Small is 0, not 'Small'. A string enum needs explicit string values.
Optional means the property may be missing or undefined, not that it may be any type. email?: string is still a string when present.

quiz.q: What does tsc produce from app.ts, and what happens to the type annotations?
quiz.a: It produces app.js. Annotations, interfaces and type aliases are removed. A non-const enum remains as a JavaScript object.

quiz.q: Why can an interface not be used with instanceof at run time?
quiz.a: Interfaces exist only during compilation. The compiler erases them, so no interface value reaches the browser. instanceof needs a real run-time value.

quiz.q: Given function add(a: number, b: number): number, does add('2', 3) compile? What does plain JavaScript return for '2' + 3?
quiz.a: It does not compile: '2' is a string, not assignable to number. Plain JavaScript returns '23' because + joins the string and the converted number.

quiz.q: A team types all server data as any to save time. Explain the risk in type-checking terms.
quiz.a: any disables checking for that value and spreads to property accesses. Misspelled fields and wrong types are accepted at compile time, so the bug appears at run time when the data is used.

quiz.q: State the difference between any and unknown.
quiz.a: any allows every operation with no check. unknown accepts any value but allows no operation until you narrow it with typeof or another check.

quiz.q: Write TypeScript types for an array of numbers and for a tuple of a string followed by a number.
quiz.a: Array of numbers: number[] or Array<number>. Tuple: [string, number]. The angle-bracket form is the generic form; both array forms are equivalent for this type.

quiz.q: Why should an exported function have a written return type even when TypeScript can infer it?
quiz.a: The written return type is a contract at the module boundary. It stops a later edit inside the function from silently changing the type callers rely on, and it documents the shape for other files.

quiz.q: Using structural typing, explain why { id: 7, name: 'Ravi' } is accepted where User is expected.
quiz.a: User requires id: number and name: string, with email optional. The object has id as number 7 and name as string 'Ravi'. The shape matches, so the object is accepted even without declaring implements User.

beyond: Not for the exam. TypeScript's type system can compute types with conditional and mapped types; libraries use them to turn a schema into types. Search 'TypeScript utility types', 'tsconfig strict', and 'type narrowing'. The Angular code in 5.6 and 5.9 relies on interfaces and generics from this chapter.
